question.value: Identify dense cores in ALMA 1.3 mm maps of 8 massive filamentary clouds, classify them as prestellar or protostellar, compare getsf and astrodendro, and derive core masses and the core mass function (CMF) and how it changes with cloud evolution

evidence.quote: To investigate the relationship between filaments and star formation, we carry out the INFANT (INvestigations of massive Filaments ANd sTar formation) survey, a multi-scale, multi-wavelength survey of massive filamentary clouds
Identifying the core population is the first step towards understanding the importance of filaments in high-mass star formation.
The observations were conducted with ALMA in Cycle 5 (Project ID 2017.1.00526.S, PI: Lu, X.), over a period from 2018 March to 2018 August.
All the targets were observed at band 6 using two 12-m array configurations, i.e., C43-1 and C43-4.

referee_caveats_inferred: Core masses depend on NH3 temperatures that come from separate VLA data not described in this paper, and the median regional temperature is used for 58 cores without a fit
The same temperature is used for dust as for NH3 gas, while prestellar and protostellar cores have systematically different temperatures, which could affect the mass comparison
Prestellar versus protostellar labels depend on outflow and warm-line detection limits, so misclassified protostellar cores would feed into the mass comparison and the prestellar CMF
CMF slopes use a single fit range (M > 1.5 Msun) with only three clouds per evolution group, so the evolutionary steepening trend is of limited significance
The completeness limit is estimated for beam-sized point sources, not for resolved cores in crowded regions
The comparison of getsf and astrodendro only tests point-like sources, and astrodendro parameters were not tuned
